Future Mobility

By: Marzanne Van den Berg | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Self-driving cars will hit our shores soon -- is South Africa prepared for this and other innovations in mobility?

Unique Selling Point:
How will a self-driving vehicle react on a South African road with its ample potholes, pedestrians and unpredictable minibus taxis? Who will be responsible in the case of an accident -- the owner or the manufacturer of the vehicle?
The future in mobility is coming -- we can't hide from it and if we don't handle it correctly, there will be chaos.
This is why mobility industry roleplayers are engaging with government and regulators to ensure that South African is ready for the future.
The future where cars drive themselves and can even check your calendar to determine where to go is not as far away as we may think.
The first fully autonomous vehicle will enter the country later this year, but to be used on a small scale only in order to gather data to prepare regulations for the vehicles.
The idea of self-driving cars alarm many people, especially after a self-driving car recently hit and killed a pedestrian in the USA.
I will examine what these autonomous vehicles look like, how they work and what is required in terms of regulations and infrastructure for them to operate in South Africa.
I will also touch on innovations in electric vehicles. These vehicles may soon be able to travel 400 km or more before needing to recharge. It's also set to become more accessible to the general public.

Summary:
Though the idea of cars driving themselves is alarming to many, few realise that a car with cruise control or lane assist is already the first steps in autonomous driving.
Though these vehicles are undoubtedly coming, it will be a long time before fully autonomous vehicles can operate on public roads in SA. Laws and infrastructure must be in place first.
The Mobility Centre for Africa is an NPO that aims to bring all roleplayers together in order to prepare South Africa for innovations in mobility.
Later this year, the Mobility Centre for Africa will start testing the first self-driving vehicle in South Africa (an electric shuttle by French manufacturer Navya) in various controlled areas such as the CSIR campus in Pretoria or the Durban beachfront promenade. It will gather data in order to help write regulations and prepare infrastructure for these vehicles. At the moment, there are no regulations that determine the nature and use of autonomous vehicles in SA.
These vehicles use cameras, sensors and lasers to read its environment and it builds up memory of routes as it drives. It also maintains a satellite connection for navigation. It brings other unexpected complications such as the need to store and secure massive volumes of data. An autonomous vehicle generates up to 4 TB of data per day as it scans and logs its surroundings.
In the long term we would require smart infrastructure, like sensors in road signs, lamp posts and lines on the road to ensure autonomous vehicles can read the surroundings.
The biggest challenges to so-called e-mobility in SA are infrastructure, cost, cyber security and the impact on job security -- I will examine each of these.

Further information:
The Mobility Centre for Africa is also busy with a project to develop and build a prototype of an electric minibus taxi that will be ready for testing in Port Elizabeth later this year. It aims to bring cheaper, greener public transport to the general public.
For now, electric vehicles are still very much for the rich only, but more affordable EVs are becoming available.
The range on EVs is also ever increasing and charging infrastructure is becoming more convenient. Public charging is available in more and more places in SA, and innovations are required to manage how these are used.
A move towards electric vehicles also raises questions about the availability and affordability of electricity and what it would mean if we became less dependent upon fuel.

Press Release:


Future Mobility
No driver's seat and no steering wheel – the future of driving is autonomous and electric. While the idea of cars controlling themselves may seem alarming to some, the first fully autonomous vehicle will arrive in South Africa by next year and the laws and infrastructure in the country will have to catch up quickly. Carte Blanche explores the future of mobility.


Script:


SCRIPT: Future Mobility
PRODUCER: Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: Claire Mawisa
EDITOR: Stenette Grosskopf
TX DATE: 24 June 2018 (TBC)

INSERT

VISUAL SEQUENCE OF PARKING PROBLEMS WITH MUSIC

VO: It’s a familiar sight -- motorists struggling to parallel park. But it may soon be a thing of the past as more cars become able to do it for themselves.

VISUAL SEQUENCE OF THE AUDI RS PARKING ITSELF WITH CLAIRE BEHIND THE WHEEL

CLAIRE laughing. NICO SMIT (off camera): So the hardest thing now is you want to take steering wheel, right? CLAIRE: Yes! NICO SMIT: You want to take control. So it’s simply a case of trust. Keep going. CLAIRE: This is a lot. NICO SMIT: You’ll see the car will start to turn back in a second. CLAIRE: This is a lot!

VO: You may think cars that drive themselves are still a distant high-tech dream for South Africans, but actually systems like park assist, cruise control and automatic lane centering are the first steps towards autonomous driving. Technology expert Arthur Goldstuck has seen the latest in vehicle innovation at tech shows around the world.

ARTHUR GOLDSTUCK, MANAGING DIRECTOR, WORLD WIDE WORX: You could almost call it a tidal wave of technology that’s coming at the car, at the automobile and that means that in the next five to ten years you’re going to see an entirely different environment.

VO: The cars of the future will be autonomous and electric.

ARTHUR GOLDSTUCK, MANAGING DIRECTOR, WORLD WIDE WORX: One of the things that you’ll see in this autonomous future is that the car becomes an office and you’ll have a meeting of two, three, four people on the way from Johannesburg to Pretoria. Your whole family will be watching a Netflix movie together in the car, for example, streaming in high definition from satellite or from roadside 5G connections.

VO: Suddenly, living in your car doesn’t sound too bad! Autonomous driving means we have to rethink everyday things like driving licences and car insurance. The Mobility Centre for Africa is a non-profit organisation set up to help South Africa prepare for the future of mobility. Victor Radebe is the executive director.

VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: As a nation, okay, we need to make a statement. We need to be sending a message that we are futuristic in our outlook.

VO: The Mobility Centre for Africa will import South Africa’s first fully autonomous electric vehicle for testing by next year.

VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: It’s an autonomous bus, 14 seater bus, okay. Nice and small. No pedals, no steering wheel, okay. It’s, uh, fully autonomous.

VO: Now, don’t panic! The autonomous shuttle bus won’t be alongside you on the N1 just yet. The plan is to operate it in controlled environments such as university campuses and beachfront promenades to gather data.

VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: So in South Africa we also want to test the public opinion. We want to get you onto a driverless vehicle, you know, and… alone with the vehicle and then you can talk to it and tell it where you want it to stop, you know.
CLAIRE MAWISA: My anxiety levels just shot up as you said…
VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: Well, we’ll have the red panic button that you can stop.
CLAIRE MAWISA: I like that, thank you. I need that.

VO: There are five levels of autonomous driving. Levels 1 and 2 include the types of driver assistance already available. Level 3 allows the driver’s attention to be elsewhere, but he or she must be ready to take control when prompted. At Level 4 the vehicle can drive itself under certain conditions and Level 5 is full autonomy.

ARTHUR GOLDSTUCK, MANAGING DIRECTOR, WORLD WIDE WORX: Most of the manufacturers have targeted 2021 as the year of the autonomous vehicle when they actually come off production lines and appear on showroom floors.

VO: Radebe believes we must act fast if we want to safeguard our vehicle manufacturing industry.

VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: The more we do those tests and research in South Africa, the more we’re paving the way for the adoption of this technology, because it’s a… it’s an imperative for us because we’re building cars for the export market.

VO: Though the technology is still in development, a spate of recent crashes in America involving Tesla and Uber vehicles with self-driving technology has fueled fears that the push to be first is putting safety last.

CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: South African roads are unpredictable and the concern most people have is how autonomous vehicles will adapt to these conditions.

VO: Trevor Hill heads up Audi South Africa, one of the vehicle manufacturers pioneering autonomous driving technology.

TREVOR HILL, HEAD OF BRAND, AUDI SOUTH AFRICA: You need very good quality roads, you need very visible lines on the roads, because the car picks up impulses and sight from the lines on the roads, and you need a very good traffic sign system.

VO: Self-driving cars use technology called Lidar or Light Detection and Ranging. It sends out pulses of laser light and measures how long it takes to bounce back in order to create a 3D image of its surroundings. The vehicles also have cameras, radar and other sensors.

VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: So the vehicle can see everywhere where you can’t see. So it can see underneath, it can see whether there’s a pothole, it can see behind it, it can see on the side. So you won’t need traffic lights for instance if a vehicle can communicate with other vehicles. So they will be giving each other right of way.

VO: The vision for the future is roads filled with autonomous vehicles, communicating with each other and sharing information through super-fast 5G mobile internet. Cars will be able to warn each other about hazards and even alert emergency services. Imagine being able to program your car to shut down or refuse to charge if it’s stolen or hijacked.

TREVOR HILL, HEAD OF BRAND, AUDI SOUTH AFRICA: People are living much older and they want to mobile much longer and all of these autonomous driving features in the car will enable our elderly people, and even the young people, to drive more efficiently and much safer for a longer period.

VO: Full autonomous driving is still illegal in South Africa and many other countries. Our Road Traffic Act says that a driver must have complete control over a vehicle.

VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: Ultimately we’re going to move to eliminating the driver completely from the driving equation because he is the problem. The driver is the problem.

VO: Self-driving cars are still a few years away, but there are already about 450 fully electric cars on our roads. Winstone Jordaan is the CEO of GridCars, which manufactures electric vehicle charge points.

CLAIRE MAWISA: Why go electric? What are the advantages of having electric vehicles?
WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: Ooo, I think... I don’t think we don’t have the time. It’s… it’s such an amazing thing. The electric motors are so simple. They’re really simple compared to fossil fuel engines. And they’re just so much quicker. The performance is better, and at the end of the day when you look at the comparison between fuel price and electric price, we’re talking about a fifth of the cost for the same amount of kilometres. You’re not going to have to go and service your car every 10 000 kilometres.

VO: One unexpected twist is the reputation that electric vehicles -- with their compact and quiet engines -- are gaining as high-tech, high-performance sports cars.

WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: We did a conversion of an old Bantam 1992 and it did 0 to 100 in 7 seconds. The minute you put your foot down to the accelerator you’ve got power immediately and that’s what makes them so ideal when it comes to sports cars and sports car technology.

CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: They’re easy to charge, affordable in the long term and a dream to drive. So why aren’t there more electric vehicles in South Africa?

VO: There’s this fear of being stranded with a flat battery and nowhere to charge, but that’s changing.

WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: The vehicles in the market are doing ranges of around 150 to 200 kilometres, maybe 250. There’s some new vehicles coming in, like the Jaguar I-PACE. They’ll be doing up to 500 kilometres on a single charge. We will see advances in the battery technology and that will help us to get more and more range on the vehicles.
CLAIRE MAWISA: How does it work? How do I pay when I want to charge my car when I’m not charging it at home?
WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: You get one of these cards and you would swipe the card against the charge point and that would then bill it against your account. So you would be able to pay for it at that point.
CLAIRE: And where are these charge points?
WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: They’re actually all over the place. So there’s about 70 of them between Pretoria and Johannesburg already.

VO: These charge points are at dealerships that sell electric vehicles and in some public places.

CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: Industry experts say this wave of mobility innovation is coming; we can’t avoid it. In fact, we have to start paddling now if we want to ride this wave. That is, if we can hear it coming...

15 secs
VO: We South Africans love our cars, but how will the cars of the future affect the way we drive?
ARTHUR GOLDSTUCK, MANAGING DIRECTOR, WORLD WIDE WORX: You could almost call it a tidal wave of technology that’s coming at the car, at the automobile.

30 secs
VO: The future where we can Netflix and chill in our cars while it drives us to our destinations is not too distant. How do self-driving cars detect other cars, pedestrians and potholes while keeping to their speed and lane? And can we trust the machines?
VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: So the vehicle can see everywhere where you can’t see. It can see whether there’s a pothole, it can see behind it, it can see on the side and in future the autonomous vehicles would be able to communicate with other vehicles, okay, so, you won’t need traffic lights for instance.

VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: As a nation, okay, we need to make a statement. We need to be sending a message that we are futuristic in our outlook. VO: The Mobility Centre for Africa will import South Africa’s first fully autonomous electric vehicle for testing by next year. VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: It’s an autonomous bus, 14 seater bus, okay. Nice and small. No pedals, no steering wheel, okay. It’s, uh, fully autonomous. VO: Now, don’t panic! The autonomous shuttle bus won’t be alongside you on the N1 just yet. The plan is to operate it in controlled environments such as university campuses and beachfront promenades to gather data. VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: So in South Africa we also want to test the public opinion. We want to get you onto a driverless vehicle, you know, and… alone with the vehicle and then you can talk to it and tell it where you want it to stop, you know. CLAIRE MAWISA: My anxiety levels just shot up as you said… VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: Well, we’ll have the red panic button that you can stop. CLAIRE MAWISA: I like that, thank you. I need that. VO: There are five levels of autonomous driving. Levels 1 and 2 include the types of driver assistance already available. Level 3 allows the driver’s attention to be elsewhere, but he or she must be ready to take control when prompted. At Level 4 the vehicle can drive itself under certain conditions and Level 5 is full autonomy. ARTHUR GOLDSTUCK, MANAGING DIRECTOR, WORLD WIDE WORX: Most of the manufacturers have targeted 2021 as the year of the autonomous vehicle when they actually come off production lines and appear on showroom floors. VO: Radebe believes we must act fast if we want to safeguard our vehicle manufacturing industry. VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: The more we do those tests and research in South Africa, the more we’re paving the way for the adoption of this technology, because it’s a… it’s an imperative for us because we’re building cars for the export market. VO: Though the technology is still in development, a spate of recent crashes in America involving Tesla and Uber vehicles with self-driving technology has fueled fears that the push to be first is putting safety last. CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: South African roads are unpredictable and the concern most people have is how autonomous vehicles will adapt to these conditions. VO: Trevor Hill heads up Audi South Africa, one of the vehicle manufacturers pioneering autonomous driving technology. TREVOR HILL, HEAD OF BRAND, AUDI SOUTH AFRICA: You need very good quality roads, you need very visible lines on the roads, because the car picks up impulses and sight from the lines on the roads, and you need a very good traffic sign system. VO: Self-driving cars use technology called Lidar or Light Detection and Ranging. It sends out pulses of laser light and measures how long it takes to bounce back in order to create a 3D image of its surroundings. The vehicles also have cameras, radar and other sensors. VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: So the vehicle can see everywhere where you can’t see. So it can see underneath, it can see whether there’s a pothole, it can see behind it, it can see on the side. So you won’t need traffic lights for instance if a vehicle can communicate with other vehicles. So they will be giving each other right of way. VO: The vision for the future is roads filled with autonomous vehicles, communicating with each other and sharing information through super-fast 5G mobile internet. Cars will be able to warn each other about hazards and even alert emergency services. Imagine being able to program your car to shut down or refuse to charge if it’s stolen or hijacked. TREVOR HILL, HEAD OF BRAND, AUDI SOUTH AFRICA: People are living much older and they want to mobile much longer and all of these autonomous driving features in the car will enable our elderly people, and even the young people, to drive more efficiently and much safer for a longer period. VO: Full autonomous driving is still illegal in South Africa and many other countries. Our Road Traffic Act says that a driver must have complete control over a vehicle. VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: Ultimately we’re going to move to eliminating the driver completely from the driving equation because he is the problem. The driver is the problem. VO: Self-driving cars are still a few years away, but there are already about 450 fully electric cars on our roads. Winstone Jordaan is the CEO of GridCars, which manufactures electric vehicle charge points. CLAIRE MAWISA: Why go electric? What are the advantages of having electric vehicles? WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: Ooo, I think... I don’t think we don’t have the time. It’s… it’s such an amazing thing. The electric motors are so simple. They’re really simple compared to fossil fuel engines. And they’re just so much quicker. The performance is better, and at the end of the day when you look at the comparison between fuel price and electric price, we’re talking about a fifth of the cost for the same amount of kilometres. You’re not going to have to go and service your car every 10 000 kilometres. VO: One unexpected twist is the reputation that electric vehicles -- with their compact and quiet engines -- are gaining as high-tech, high-performance sports cars. WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: We did a conversion of an old Bantam 1992 and it did 0 to 100 in 7 seconds. The minute you put your foot down to the accelerator you’ve got power immediately and that’s what makes them so ideal when it comes to sports cars and sports car technology. CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: They’re easy to charge, affordable in the long term and a dream to drive. So why aren’t there more electric vehicles in South Africa? VO: There’s this fear of being stranded with a flat battery and nowhere to charge, but that’s changing. WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: The vehicles in the market are doing ranges of around 150 to 200 kilometres, maybe 250. There’s some new vehicles coming in, like the Jaguar I-PACE. They’ll be doing up to 500 kilometres on a single charge. We will see advances in the battery technology and that will help us to get more and more range on the vehicles. CLAIRE MAWISA: How does it work? How do I pay when I want to charge my car when I’m not charging it at home? WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: You get one of these cards and you would swipe the card against the charge point and that would then bill it against your account. So you would be able to pay for it at that point. CLAIRE: And where are these charge points? WINSTONE JORDAAN, DIRECTOR, GRIDCARS: They’re actually all over the place. So there’s about 70 of them between Pretoria and Johannesburg already. VO: These charge points are at dealerships that sell electric vehicles and in some public places. CLAIRE MAWISA LINK: Industry experts say this wave of mobility innovation is coming; we can’t avoid it. In fact, we have to start paddling now if we want to ride this wave. That is, if we can hear it coming... PROMOS 10 secs VO: Vehicles with self-driving technology are already here. With our notoriously unpredictable roads, is South Africa ready for this revolution? 15 secs VO: Would you feel confident to sit back and read a book while your car drives itself? VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: Ultimately we’re going to move to eliminating the driver completely from the driving equation because he is the problem. The driver is the problem. 15 secs VO: We South Africans love our cars, but how will the cars of the future affect the way we drive? ARTHUR GOLDSTUCK, MANAGING DIRECTOR, WORLD WIDE WORX: You could almost call it a tidal wave of technology that’s coming at the car, at the automobile. 30 secs VO: The future where we can Netflix and chill in our cars while it drives us to our destinations is not too distant. How do self-driving cars detect other cars, pedestrians and potholes while keeping to their speed and lane? And can we trust the machines? VICTOR RADEBE, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, MOBILITY CENTRE FOR AFRICA: So the vehicle can see everywhere where you can’t see. It can see whether there’s a pothole, it can see behind it, it can see on the side and in future the autonomous vehicles would be able to communicate with other vehicles, okay, so, you won’t need traffic lights for instance.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Self-driving cars will hit our shores soon -- is South Africa prepared for this and other innovations in mobility?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: How will a self-driving vehicle react on a South African road with its ample potholes, pedestrians and unpredictable minibus taxis? Who will be responsible in the case of an accident -- the owner or the manufacturer of the vehicle? The future in mobility is coming -- we can't hide from it and if we don't handle it correctly, there will be chaos. This is why mobility industry roleplayers are engaging with government and regulators to ensure that South African is ready for the future. The future where cars drive themselves and can even check your calendar to determine where to go is not as far away as we may think. The first fully autonomous vehicle will enter the country later this year, but to be used on a small scale only in order to gather data to prepare regulations for the vehicles. The idea of self-driving cars alarm many people, especially after a self-driving car recently hit and killed a pedestrian in the USA. I will examine what these autonomous vehicles look like, how they work and what is required in terms of regulations and infrastructure for them to operate in South Africa. I will also touch on innovations in electric vehicles. These vehicles may soon be able to travel 400 km or more before needing to recharge. It's also set to become more accessible to the general public.
metadata.Summary: Though the idea of cars driving themselves is alarming to many, few realise that a car with cruise control or lane assist is already the first steps in autonomous driving. Though these vehicles are undoubtedly coming, it will be a long time before fully autonomous vehicles can operate on public roads in SA. Laws and infrastructure must be in place first. The Mobility Centre for Africa is an NPO that aims to bring all roleplayers together in order to prepare South Africa for innovations in mobility. Later this year, the Mobility Centre for Africa will start testing the first self-driving vehicle in South Africa (an electric shuttle by French manufacturer Navya) in various controlled areas such as the CSIR campus in Pretoria or the Durban beachfront promenade. It will gather data in order to help write regulations and prepare infrastructure for these vehicles. At the moment, there are no regulations that determine the nature and use of autonomous vehicles in SA. These vehicles use cameras, sensors and lasers to read its environment and it builds up memory of routes as it drives. It also maintains a satellite connection for navigation. It brings other unexpected complications such as the need to store and secure massive volumes of data. An autonomous vehicle generates up to 4 TB of data per day as it scans and logs its surroundings. In the long term we would require smart infrastructure, like sensors in road signs, lamp posts and lines on the road to ensure autonomous vehicles can read the surroundings. The biggest challenges to so-called e-mobility in SA are infrastructure, cost, cyber security and the impact on job security -- I will examine each of these.
metadata.Further information: The Mobility Centre for Africa is also busy with a project to develop and build a prototype of an electric minibus taxi that will be ready for testing in Port Elizabeth later this year. It aims to bring cheaper, greener public transport to the general public. For now, electric vehicles are still very much for the rich only, but more affordable EVs are becoming available. The range on EVs is also ever increasing and charging infrastructure is becoming more convenient. Public charging is available in more and more places in SA, and innovations are required to manage how these are used. A move towards electric vehicles also raises questions about the availability and affordability of electricity and what it would mean if we became less dependent upon fuel.
